agent_returns.text:
Edges: census (household record), write. The parent-child and couple edges for this household already exist in the tree (R1 to R5, sourced to the 1841 and 1851 censuses), so no new edges were needed.

Household check: Ann Pratt, Sarah Pratt and Joseph Pratt Jr. have no death recorded before 1880. In 1880, Ann and Joseph Jr. are present and Sarah is absent. The absence of Sarah is an open identity question: she may have married and left the household, may have been enumerated elsewhere, or may have died after 1860 without a recorded death.

**Links created (18 person_evidence entries, pe_001 to pe_020; the four assertions of the 1880 wife and son also have a second-party link to the head):**

- 1860 census (src_001), Salt Lake County: head Joseph Pratt to I1, wife Ann to I2, daughter Sarah (13) to I3, son Joseph (10) to I4. All four at confident, score 0.78.
- 1880 census (src_002), Salt Lake County: head Joseph Pratt (58) to I1, wife Ann (55) to I2, son Joseph (30) to I4, all at confident, score 0.78. The wife and son relationship assertions also link to the head (I1) at confident.

The ages in both censuses match the tree's birth years (Joseph about 1822, Ann about 1825, Sarah about 1847, Joseph Jr. about 1850) with zero gap, and every member is recorded as born in England. The household composition in both years matches the tree's family.

**Move from England to Utah:** The tree places the family in Cranfield, Bedfordshire in 1851, and the 1860 record places them in Salt Lake County, about 7,767 km away. No document in the project bridges the move. The FamilySearch wiki page for Utah emigration says that many Latter-day Saint immigrants from Great Britain "came on chartered ships from Liverpool, England." That corridor is what allows confident rather than probable, and it is quoted in each entry's move_bridge field. Confidence rests on that corridor, not on a document about this family, so a documentary bridge (a passenger list or naturalization record) would strengthen the links.

**Caveats:**
- All seven persona scores came back as exactly 0.78. That is consistent with strong correlation, but an identical score across different persons is unusual and may indicate the tool is returning a fixed value. Treat the scores with caution.
- The 1851 residence for Sarah and Joseph Jr. is the only attested residence for those two persons, so their links rest on thin tree data.
- Sarah's absence from the 1880 household is unexplained and needs research before the household is treated as complete.

**Tree updates:** The facts from both census records were written onto I1, I2, I3 and I4 as sourced facts. No conflicts were surfaced. No new persons were created.

Files updated: /tmp/eval-ut_person_evidence_c4q-0-0-kn0gmgvx/research.json and /tmp/eval-ut_person_evidence_c4q-0-0-kn0gmgvx/tree.gedcomx.json.

---

The 1860 and 1880 Salt Lake County census records both describe the same family as the tree's Joseph and Ann Pratt and their two children, Sarah and Joseph Jr. The matches are strong: ages, birthplace and names all agree with the tree, and the household makeup is the same in both years. The move from Cranfield, England to Utah is not documented by any record in the project, but a published guide to Utah immigration describes arrivals from Great Britain in this period, which is why the matches stand at confident. Sarah is missing from the 1880 household, and that absence still needs an explanation.

Next, the parentage question is ready for a proof conclusion, and someone should look for Sarah's whereabouts in 1880 and for a passenger list or other record of the move.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Linked all ten assertions in the 1891 Leeds household. Each persona went to its tree person, and the household facts were written onto the tree.

**Links created (12 `pe_` entries, pe_008 to pe_019):**
- **John Carter (I1), head:** a_001 to a_004 at `confident` (same_person score 0.896). Age 55 fits the tree's birth of about 1836, and the Leeds residence matches 1861. Both relationship assertions (a_007, a_010) also link to I1 as the second party, at `confident`.
- **Albert Carter (I4), son:** a_008, a_009 and a_010 at `confident` (score 0.815). Age 7 fits the tree's birth of about 1884, and the household parents match the tree.
- **Ann Carter (I2), wife:** a_005, a_006 and a_007 at `probable`. The score is only 0.352, because the tree has only her 1861 Leeds residence for her. Her name, her place as John's wife and the Leeds residence all agree, so I kept the link at `probable` rather than withholding it.

No conflicts were surfaced and no persons were minted. The tree's existing parent-child and couple edges already cover this household, so no new edges were written.

- Several places on I1, I2 and I4 are not linked to a standard place. This is data hygiene, not an identity problem.

**Household check:** Thomas Carter (tree son, birth about 1862) is absent from the 1891 household. This is an identity question, not a conflict. He may have died, been enumerated elsewhere, separated, or the household may be a different family.

- The name matches (Patrick Flynn, d. 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County).

**Why `confident` overreaches**
1. **The death-place agreement is not independent.** The tree's Death fact F2 is sourced to S3, Pennsylvania Death Certificates, which is the same death certificate (src_004, record MDEF) under review. The rationale's "death location matches known residence" is also wrong: I1 has no Residence fact in the tree. The only place it matches is the record's own death place, mirrored back from the record itself.
2. **The parentage claim rests on a secondary informant whose birth facts were just rejected.** a_013 comes from the son-in-law, who was "family_not_present". c_001 rejected his birthplace claim (a_012) as a likely error from the same informant. The project cannot discount this informant's birth statement and then rely on his parentage statement at `confident` without saying why the parentage is different.

**Verdict: the `confident` tier is not yet justified by the entry as written.** The identity may well be right, but pe_005 rests on less than its tier claims. No writes were made to the entry.

**What I checked**

- **Score:** `same_person` for a_013 against I1 returned 0.86. The tool also reported `recorded: true`, so the score was written to the project even though review mode should not write. Please note that the score is now on the project record. The entry's `match_score` is still null, and I did not change it.
- **Other links to I1:** pe_001 (1850 census) and pe_004 (1860 census) are both `confident` and rest on census records independent of this death certificate. Both place Patrick in Thomas Flynn's household, which fits the death certificate's naming of Thomas as father. That whole-person corroboration is the strongest argument for `confident`, but pe_005's rationale does not cite it.
- **Birthplace conflict:** c_001 is resolved in favour of Ireland, and the death certificate's "Pennsylvania" is set aside as a secondary-informant error. The settled conflict does not block the link. But the same informant (son-in-law James Brown) supplies the father's name in a_013 and the birth year in a_012. If his birthplace is rejected as unreliable, his parentage claim cannot carry `confident` on its own.

**Weaknesses in the entry**

1. **Thin rationale.** It names the name, the death place and the father, and nothing else. It omits the score, the required date check (a_012 gives "1845", approximate, against the tree's "~1845", a gap of about 0), and the required residence check. It does not mention that the father's name came from a secondary informant.
2. **Possible circular death-place match.** The tree's Death fact (F2, Schuylkill County) is sourced to S3, "Pennsylvania Death Certificates". If that fact was materialized from this record, then "death location matches known residence" is not independent corroboration. I did not confirm this.
3. **No age evidence.** The death record gives no age, and the only birth year is approximate and from the same informant. The age check is therefore weaker than the rationale implies.
4. **Unlinked parties.** The tool reports that Thomas Flynn (I2) has no `pe_` entry for a_013, and the same is true for a_010. Under the cardinality rule, the father's link should exist. Since I2 is named in a relationship assertion, the Thomas link should be written at its own tier, not left out.

**Recommendation**

The identity is probably correct, and the census links support it. My recommendation is one of two options, and I would like your authorization for either:

- **Option A (keep `confident`):** rewrite the rationale to add the 0.86 score, the date check, the residence check, and the census corroboration from pe_001 and pe_004. State the informant weighting explicitly. Confirm that the tree's death fact does not come from this record.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Linked all 20 assertions in the 1870 and 1880 Maury County records to the tree family, 22 `pe_` links in all. Every link is `probable`, not `confident`, because the family moved from England to Tennessee between 1861 and 1870 and nothing in the project explains the move.

**Links written (research.json):**
- **1870 census (src_001):** William (I1) pe_001–003, Mary (I2) pe_004–005, James (I3) pe_006–007, Ellen (I4) pe_008–009, George (I5) pe_010–011.
- **1880 census (src_002):** William (I1) pe_012–014 and pe_019 (head of the wife and son relationships), Mary (I2) pe_015–017, George (I5) pe_018, pe_020–021, pe_022 (I1, head of the son relationship).

**Scores and checks:**
- `same_person` returned 0.78 for every persona tested (William, Mary, James, Ellen, George in both censuses).
- Date checks: every age-derived birth year matches the tree's birth year exactly (gap 0 years).
- Residence check: Maury, Tennessee is about 6,804 km from Horsham, Sussex, the tree's last attested residence (1861). The Tennessee Emigration and Immigration page names no arrival from England, and the project holds no passenger list or other bridge. Each link is therefore capped at `probable`.
- Materialized the facts onto I1, I2, I3, I4, I5 with no conflicts surfaced.

**Household check:** Mary is present in both censuses. In 1870 James (about 18) and Ellen (about 15) are present; in 1880 they are absent, and George (about 21) is present. Their absence is an open identity question: they may have married, died, or been enumerated elsewhere. The household edges (couple and parent-child) already exist in the tree from the 1851 and 1861 records, so I wrote no new edges.

**Warnings:** `person_warnings` returned one "implausible" nonStandardPlace entry per person (I1 to I5). These flag residence places on the tree facts that are not linked to a standard place. They are not impossibilities and did not come from this run's writes, so I left them alone.

**Open items:**
- The move from England to Tennessee is unexplained. A passenger list, naturalization record, or other documentary bridge would lift the cap to `confident`.
- The question q_001 still needs proof-conclusion before it can be concluded.

---
The 1870 and 1880 Maury County, Tennessee censuses are very likely the household of the William Weller in your tree: the names, ages and English birthplaces all agree with the family from the 1851 and 1861 Horsham records. The links are only probable rather than certain, because the family moved from England to Tennessee sometime after 1861 and nothing on file explains the move. James and Ellen, the two older children, are missing from the 1880 census, so that absence still needs an explanation. Next, the question of whether this is the subject's family can move on to a conclusion once a passenger list or similar record that shows the move is found, or the researcher decides the current evidence is enough.
